title: The First Declension — Masculine
subtitle: ὁ ποιητής, ὁ νεανίας — masculine forms in the first declension.
objectives: Decline first-declension masculine nouns in all five cases and both numbers.
Recognize that these nouns take the masculine article despite first-declension endings.
Distinguish the masculine nominative singular -ης or -ας from the feminine.
Parse first-declension masculine nouns on sight.

sections.heading: Masculine nouns in the first declension
sections.body:
Most first-declension nouns are feminine. A small group is masculine. These nouns follow the first-declension pattern in the singular but take masculine plural endings borrowed from the second declension. They always take the masculine article: ὁ ποιητής, not ἡ ποιητής.

The nominative singular ends in -ης or -ας. The genitive singular ends in -ου (like the second declension). The dative singular ends in -ῃ or -ᾳ (like the feminine). The accusative singular ends in -ην or -αν. The vocative singular ends in -ᾰ (short α).

The plural uses second-declension masculine endings: -αι, -ῶν, -αις, -ᾱς.

sections.heading: The paradigm: ὁ ποιητής (poet)
sections.body:
singular        plural
  nominative  ποιητής         ποιηταί
  genitive    ποιητοῦ         ποιητῶν
  dative      ποιητῇ          ποιηταῖς
  accusative  ποιητήν         ποιητάς
  vocative    ποιητά          ποιηταί

With the masculine article:
  nominative  ὁ ποιητής       οἱ ποιηταί
  genitive    τοῦ ποιητοῦ     τῶν ποιητῶν
  dative      τῷ ποιητῇ       τοῖς ποιηταῖς
  accusative  τὸν ποιητήν     τοὺς ποιητάς
  vocative    ὦ ποιητά        ὦ ποιηταί

Notice the vocative singular: ποιητά (short α, no circumflex). This is the distinctive marker of first-declension masculines.

sections.heading: The paradigm: ὁ νεανίας (young man)
sections.body:
singular        plural
  nominative  νεανίας         νεανίαι
  genitive    νεανίου         νεανιῶν
  dative      νεανίᾳ          νεανίαις
  accusative  νεανίαν         νεανίας
  vocative    νεανία          νεανίαι

Long α throughout the singular (after ι). Genitive singular still ends in -ου (masculine).

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Cover the answers. Parse each form or answer each question.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 2.7 introduces the genitive case. You have seen the genitive ending in every declension, but now we examine its function: possession, source, separation, partitive, and more. The genitive is the most versatile case in Greek.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can decline ὁ ποιητής and ὁ νεανίας from memory and can distinguish masculine from feminine first-declension forms on sight.
